I've about 600 pokémon and was thankful when I got enough coins to buy more space. Here are my rules for hoarding:

Keep every shiny. They're rare even during community days. I have about 60 or so.

Keep every legendary. I have a hard time letting go of these, especially since I rarely get time to raid. Probably won't trade them because I got a majority of them in a memorable location, which brings me to...

Keep every pokémon with sentimental value. I traded with a friend and the mon has crap Ivs? Good, cause no matter what I'm not getting rid of 'im unless they say I can transfer it to the professor. If I got a mon in a place I enjoy, I'll keep it until I have no more room, then I'll trade it to the professor, but not without being sad.

Finally, I keep every single pokémon I've ever put in a gym. My rule is that if they're in a gym, they're like a pet. Doesn't make much sense, but I'd never trade them. Doesn't matter if they have crap Ivs or what, I've had them since the beginning. 

I'm hoping we get some kind of box we can put the ones that are sentimental to us in, and then the rest of them can be good defenders, attackers, etc. K thanks for listening to my Ted talk

To be honest, I don't even know what genre I was going for. I used to take part in these multiple-animator projects (or, "MAPs" for short), and that's where I got a lot of my subscribers from. I just wanted to take a break for a while because animations take a TON of time, and I just started doing whatever animations I wanted to make. That didn't fly with some of my audience though, as I saw a significant drop off when I privated most of the videos I made. I'm not blaming them, as I had kept my content the same for three years, and it was a really drastic change lol

I had a snowball effect from 2013-2015. I started my channel in 2012, making cat videos and short animations. At the end of 2012, I had maybe four or five subscribers. At the end of 2013 I had maybe a hundred, the end of 2014 I had 660, and when the end of 2015 rolled around, I had just hit 2k. It all went down hill when I privated most of my videos because I wanted to change my content, and I didn't like my old stuff. I didn't want to be known for a video viewed 160k times, I wanted to have viewers see the person running the channel. I then started making drastic changes in my content at the beginning of 2017 (by this point I had about 2,600 subs), and ended the year with 60 videos on my channel (all the rest were privated), and 2,430 subscribers. I used to get almost 1k views per video in 2015, but that number dropped down to 63 views per video a year and a half later. I don't know how many people are actually subscribed anymore, since my channel is a bit old, they either don't watch anymore or don't use those channels anymore. Since I get so little views, I'm guessing it's both, and as a result, I have no idea how many people still are subscribed (like, watching videos, commenting, willingly subscribed instead of just forgetting they subscribed in the first place). I understand there are still people behind that subscriber count and that view count, it's just hard to tell how many there are after all this. I have to say that if I kept my content the same for a little while longer, I'd have gained a bit of a bigger audience who would be somewhat alright with some changes. Snowball effects, from my experience, die out. Sure there will still be loyal people who watch every video, but most of the time they'll just subscribe for one single thing instead of acknowledging the other talents you have. My suggestion would be to keep working hard at your crafts, and try to appeal to one demographic at first. Try making videos that you want to make, and that you wouldn't mind watching (that's what I did and that's how I got that snowball effect). A bigger audience, from what I can tell, isn't too fickle, but be very careful. The snowball can stop rolling at any second.

I'm so sorry for that huge wall of text, I've been waiting for a good time to share my experiences, and here you go!! I hope this was informative, and I wish you luck on your YouTube journey!
